newsitem.title: USA: Authorities reopen probe into 1963 church bombing.
newsitem.headline: Authorities reopen probe into 1963 church bombing.

text.p: Federal agents and local police have reopened an investigation into the 1963 bombing of Birmingham's 16th Street Baptist Church that killed four girls, the Washington Post reported in Thursday editions.

The newspaper quoted law enforcement officials as saying they had received new information more than a year ago about the Sept. 15, 1963 attack, which is featured in a new Spike Lee film "Four Girls" that opened in New York this week.

Based on the tip and an extensive review of FBI and state investigative files, the FBI, local police and state and federal prosecutors concluded that they had enough evidence to reopen the investigation.

"The investigation is ongoing and we are pursuing a number of leads," Craig Dahle, a spokesman for the FBI's Birmingham office, told the paper, adding that officials believed "there existed sufficient basis to reopen this investigation so that all persons responsible for this heinous crime would finally be brought to justice."
Law enforcment officials familiar with the case said the probe has developed suspects who are under investigation.
One 11-year old girl and three 14-year-olds attending Sunday school were killed when a bomb was hurled out of a car passing by the church that September day 34 years ago.

Another 14 people were injured, holes were blown in the church walls and at least five cars were damaged in the attack, which sparked further confrontations in the streets of Birmingham and became a seminal moment in the civil rights movement.
The day of the attack, civil rights leader Martin Luther King, Jr., sent President John Kennedy a telegram pleading for he before a bloody race war developed.

Only one man, R.E. Chambliss was ever brought to trial for the bombing and he received a life sentence in 1977, dying in prison in 1985. Two other suspects were cited by investigators as being in the car with Chambliss when the dynamite was planted, but there was never sufficient evidence to bring them to trial.
